place.zh: 石坳村 · 你家 · 傍晚

setup.zh: 马三踹开柴门：还差一张鹿皮、二十斤肉，立冬那天晌午来拿，拿不着，墙上那张弓就归他。马小宝要你学狗叫。
setup.en: Ma San kicks the gate open: a deer hide and twenty jin of meat still owed; he will come for them at noon on the Start of Winter, and if they are not there, the bow on the wall is his. Ma Xiaobao wants you to bark like a dog.

recap.zh: 马三来收租：还差一张鹿皮、二十斤肉，不然拿走爷爷的弓；马小宝推了你一把，碗碎了。
recap.en: Ma San came for the rent — a deer hide and twenty jin of meat, or grandfather's bow; Ma Xiaobao shoved you and a bowl broke.

zh: 马三来了，一脚踹开柴门。
他的目光，落在墙上那张旧弓上。
en: Ma San comes, and kicks the gate open.
"Still short a deer hide and twenty jin of meat."
His eyes settle on the old bow on the wall.

label.en: The old bow on the wall

text.zh: 弓背裂过两回，拿牛筋一圈一圈缠着，是爷爷传下来的；马三的眼睛，已在它上头停了两回。
text.en: The bow-back has split twice and is bound round and round with ox sinew — your grandfather's. Ma San's eyes have come to rest on it twice already.

text.zh: 灶台上四只碗，三只缺口，只一只是囫囵的，偏偏搁在最边上。
text.en: Four bowls on the stove: three chipped, one whole — and the whole one sits right on the edge.

text.zh: 短棍包着铁皮，棍头磨得发亮；这根棍子打过的人，只怕比你认得的人还多。
text.en: The club is sheathed in iron, its head rubbed bright. It has likely struck more people than you have ever met.

story.zh:
收租的是马三。这马三是马家老爷的远房侄子，长得跟一扇门似的——其实说他像门，还是抬举了门，他本人比沈家那扇门还像门，沈家的门好歹还有几道缝。

他进屋须得侧着身子，侧了身子还得低头，低了头还得先吸一口气。

他腰里别着一根包了铁皮的短棍，这根棍子在石坳村比他本人还有名，走到哪儿，哪儿的狗便不叫了；走到哪儿，哪儿的人便忽然想起来，家里的鸡好像还没喂。

那天傍晚，天边的云忽然一暗，一阵狂风卷着落叶灌进村来，村口的狗一齐闭上了嘴，树上的麻雀排着队，一只接一只地飞走了。小满放下手里的柴刀，叹了口气，心里知道，**他**来了。

只听得「砰」的一声大响，沈家的柴门飞了出去，在半空里转了三个圈子，姿态倒也优美，不偏不倚，落在隔壁阿禾家的菜地里，砸扁了一颗白菜。

不是别的白菜，正是早上阿禾守着的那一颗——那颗白菜，阿禾家足足种了一个秋天，八十一天，一百六十二瓢水。

门口站着一个人，把夕阳挡得严严实实，正是马三。他身后又转出一个圆滚滚的身影来，每走一步，地面便要抖上一抖——主要是他自己在抖。

这人叫马小宝，是马三的独子，比小满大两岁，重小满一倍，穿一身绸子，走起路来活像一只成了精的糯米团子，手里捏着一块桂花糕。

马三拿短棍一下一下地敲着门框，敲得颇有节奏，拖长了声音道：「山——租——」话音未落，小满他爹已扑通一声跪倒，叫道：「三爷！」马三道：「我还没说完。」他爹道：「我先跪着。您慢慢说。」

马三倒愣了一愣，显是收了这许多年租，头一回碰上这般配合的。

他这才接着道：「……还差一张鹿皮，二十斤肉。」说到这里，一双眼睛在屋里转了一圈，转过墙角接水的盆，转过灶台上的碗，最后落在墙上那张缠着牛筋的旧弓上，「立冬那天晌午，我来拿。拿不着——那张弓，我就收了。」

小满他爹急道：「三爷！那是我爹传给我的！」马三伸手拍了拍他的肩膀，语重心长地道：「你爹传给你，你传给我。传承嘛。我懂。」

小满在一旁听着，心里算了一算：照这么个传法，三爷倒成了我爹的儿子、我的哥哥了。这个便宜，他占得倒是一点也不嫌亏。

便在这时，马小宝一摇一摆，绕过他爹，走到小满面前，把那块桂花糕举到了小满的鼻子底下。那一刻，时候竟像是变慢了。

小满瞧见那块糕上每一粒桂花都在发光，金灿灿的，像撒了一层碎金子；那股香味从他鼻孔里钻进去，顺着喉咙往下滑，一路滑到他空了一整天的肚子里，在那里转了一圈，挥了挥手，又走了。

他甚至听见那块桂花糕在跟他说话，它说的是：**你配吗？**

马小宝道：「沈小满，想吃吗？学声狗叫，给你舔一口。」
story.en:
The rent collector was Ma San, Master Ma's distant nephew, built like a door — in fact, calling him a door flattered the door; he was more of a door than the Shens' own, which at least had a few cracks in it.

To come into a house he had to turn sideways, then duck, then take a breath first.

At his belt hung a short iron-bound club, more famous in Shi'ao Village than the man himself: wherever it went, the dogs stopped barking; wherever it went, people suddenly remembered they hadn't fed the chickens.

That evening the clouds on the horizon darkened all at once; a gust swept a flurry of leaves into the village; the dogs at the gate shut their mouths as one, and the sparrows lined up and flew off one after another. Xiaoman put down his chopper, sighed, and knew: **he** had come.

With a great *bang* the Shens' wicker gate flew off, turned three circles in mid-air — not without grace — and came down squarely in Ahe's family's vegetable plot next door, flattening a cabbage.

Not just any cabbage: the very one Ahe had been guarding that morning — the cabbage her family had grown a whole autumn, eighty-one days and a hundred and sixty-two ladles of water.

In the doorway stood a man who blocked out the setting sun entirely: Ma San. Behind him rolled a round figure, and with each step the ground gave a wobble — mostly it was he who wobbled.

This was Ma Xiaobao, Ma San's only son, two years older than Xiaoman and twice his weight, dressed all in silk, waddling like a glutinous-rice ball come to life, a piece of osmanthus cake in his hand.

Ma San rapped the doorframe with his club, rap by rap, with a certain rhythm, and drawled: "Mountain — rent —" Before the words were out, Xiaoman's father had dropped to his knees with a thump: "Third Master!"

Ma San said, "I'm not finished." His father said, "I'll kneel first. Take your time." Ma San was taken aback: in all his years of collecting rent it was plainly the first time he'd met such cooperation.

Only then did he go on: "…Still one deer hide and twenty jin of meat short." His eyes went once round the room, past the basins catching drips in the corner, past the bowls on the stove, and came to rest on the old sinew-wrapped bow on the wall. "Noon on the Start of Winter, I'll come for it. If I don't get it — that bow is mine."

Xiaoman's father cried, "Third Master! My father handed that down to me!" Ma San reached out, patted him on the shoulder, and said, earnest and heartfelt: "Your father handed it to you, you hand it to me. It's called inheritance. I get it."

Xiaoman, listening to one side, did a sum in his head: by that line of inheritance, Third Master was his father's son, and his own elder brother. A bargain the man didn't seem to mind taking at all.

Just then Ma Xiaobao waddled round his father, stopped in front of Xiaoman, and held the osmanthus cake up under his nose. At that moment time itself seemed to slow.

Xiaoman saw every osmanthus flower on the cake shine, golden, as if dusted with gold leaf; the smell went up his nose, slid down his throat, slid all the way down into a belly empty all day, took one turn around it, waved, and left.

He even heard the cake speak to him. What it said was: **Are you worthy?**

Ma Xiaobao said, "Shen Xiaoman — want some? Bark like a dog, and you get a lick."

exits.means: talks back by parroting his words, does not bark and does not hit back

what.zh: 推你撞上灶台，摔碎了家里四只碗里的一只。
what.en: Shoved you into the stove and broke one of your family's four bowls.

story.zh:
小满便学着他的腔调道：「沈小满，想吃吗？学声狗叫，给你舔一口。」马小宝一怔，道：「……什么？」小满也一怔，道：「什么？」马小宝道：「你学不学？」小满道：「正在学。」

屋里登时静了下来。门口不知什么时候已围了半个村子的人，阿禾抱着那颗扁了的白菜，肩膀一抽一抽的。马三的脸先是红，跟着变紫，又跟着变黑，最后变成了一种颜色，小满他娘后来说，那颜色叫作「**完了**」。

马三短棍往地上一跺，喝道：「**敢戏弄我儿子！**」马小宝这才回过神来，气得浑身的肉都在抖，抢上来伸手便推了小满一把。

小满往后便倒。倒下去的那一霎之间，脑子里闪过了许许多多东西：他这十二年短暂而贫穷的一生，他爹的膝盖，他娘的手，村口那棵他爬过一百遍的老槐树，还有灶台上那四只碗。

千头万绪，到了嘴边，只剩一句，他没敢出声，在心里骂得极响：**你爷爷的。**

背心一痛，已撞上了灶台，只听得「啪」的一声，灶沿上那只碗给震了下来，在半空里滴溜溜地翻了两个筋斗。其时夕阳正从门口斜照进来，碗沿上白光一闪，倒像是在跟他作别。

小满急忙伸手去捞，说时迟那时快，指尖堪堪够到碗底，却终究差了那么一寸。

「啪嚓」一声，碗在地上碎成了七八片。

小满仰面躺在地下，望着屋顶那个窟窿，一时竟忘了起身。恰好一滴雨从窟窿里漏将下来，不偏不倚，正落在他眉心，凉飕飕的。他对着屋顶叹了口气，说道：「那是我家四只碗里，唯一一只没缺口的。」

马三一挥手，带着马小宝走了。临出门时，马小宝回过头来，冲小满挤了挤眼睛，当着他的面，把那块桂花糕一口塞进嘴里，腮帮子鼓得像两个包子。沈家的门，还躺在阿禾家的菜地里。

小满他娘蹲下身来，一片一片地捡碗的碎片。他爹在旁搓着手，道：「他娘……碗碎了，可以再买……」他娘道：「拿什么买？」他爹道：「……拿……拿我的膝盖？」他娘道：「你的膝盖，值几个钱？」

他爹认认真真地想了一想，道：「阴天的时候，挺准的。能当个天气预报。」

他娘没有笑。她就那么蹲着，手里捏着一片碗，许久没有动。他爹也不说话了，慢慢地蹲下去，挨着她，和她一起捡。两个人一片一片，捡得极慢极慢，倒像是捡得快了，那只碗便当真没了。

那七八片，他娘拿一块旧布包了，四个角系好，没有扔，收进了炕头的木箱里。一只碎了的碗，留着能做什么，那天谁也没有问。

那天夜里，小满对着屋顶的窟窿，很小很小声地说了一句：「有一天，我要让我娘，一辈子不用蹲在地上捡东西。」屋顶自然没有回答，只有一滴雨漏将下来，落进墙角的第十七个盆里，「叮」的一声。

隔着一道布帘，爹娘在低声说话。

他爹道：「……立冬是哪天？」他娘道：「大后天。」停了一停，又道：「还剩三天。」他爹道：「前山空了。只剩黑松岭。」布帘那边静了好一会儿，他娘道：「你爹，就是在黑松岭没的。」他爹道：「我知道。」他娘便不说了。

过了一会儿，她哭了一小会儿，又不哭了。

小满躺在炕上，一笔一笔地算账——这是他娘教的，他娘说，遇事先算账。

马小宝比他高一个头，重他一倍，打起来，是他输；就算他打赢了，门口还站着马三，打起来，是他爹挨揍；就算他连马三也打赢了……小满想了一想这副光景：十二岁的沈小满，一拳把一扇门打倒在地。

他觉得这个「就算」，未免有点太远了。所以今天他没还手，只回了一句嘴。回嘴不算还手，这是他给自己定的规矩。

他在黑暗里睁着眼睛，把马小宝推他那一下，马三瞧那张弓的眼神，那只飞出去的碗，还有他娘停在半空的手，一样一样都记了下来。马三，马小宝，马家老爷，还有马家老爷那个做书吏的远房表侄，他在心里挨个儿又骂了一遍：**你爷爷的。**

骂完了，又对自己说了五个字：**现在打不过。**说完一遍，又单把末了两个字念了一遍：**现在。**

到了半夜，布帘那边窸窸窣窣一阵响，他爹摸黑出去了，回来时手里多了一样沉甸甸的东西，搁在门槛上，「咚」的一声。跟着便是「嚓、嚓、嚓」，一声一声，又慢又匀，是铁在石头上磨。

沈家的磨刀石前年便裂成了两半，这一块，不知是打哪家借来的。小满数着那「嚓嚓」声，数到三百多下，数乱了，便不数了。他知道他爹在磨什么。前山已经空了，三天里要打着一头鹿，他爹磨的，是进深山的箭。
story.en:
So Xiaoman, copying his tone, said: "Shen Xiaoman — want some? Bark like a dog, and you get a lick." Ma Xiaobao blinked. "…What?" Xiaoman blinked too. "What?" Ma Xiaobao said, "Are you going to copy or not?" Xiaoman said, "I'm copying."

The room went silent. Half the village had gathered at the door, and Ahe, clutching the flattened cabbage, was shaking at the shoulders. Ma San's face went red, then purple, then black, and at last a colour that Xiaoman's mother later said was called "**done for**."

Ma San stamped his club on the floor and roared, "**You dare make a fool of my son!**" Ma Xiaobao came to himself, every inch of him quivering with rage, lunged, and shoved Xiaoman hard.

Xiaoman fell backwards. In the instant of falling a great many things flashed through his head: the short, poor twelve years of his life, his father's knee, his mother's hands, the old locust tree at the village gate he'd climbed a hundred times, and the four bowls on the stove.

A thousand threads, and by the time they reached his lips only one was left; he didn't dare say it aloud, but in his head he cursed it at the top of his voice: **Your grandpa's.**

Pain in his back — he'd struck the stove, and with a *crack* the bowl on its edge was jolted off and went tumbling head over heels through the air. The setting sun slanted in through the doorway just then; a flash of white ran round the bowl's rim, as though it were saying goodbye.

Xiaoman grabbed for it, quick as you like, and his fingertips just reached the bottom of it — and fell short by an inch.

*Crash* — the bowl broke into seven or eight pieces on the floor.

Xiaoman lay flat on his back, staring up at the hole in the roof, and for a moment forgot to get up. Just then a drop of rain leaked through the hole and landed squarely between his eyebrows, cold. He sighed at the roof and said, "That was the only one of our four bowls without a chip."

Ma San waved a hand and went, taking Ma Xiaobao with him. At the door Ma Xiaobao turned, winked at Xiaoman, and right in front of him stuffed the whole osmanthus cake into his mouth, cheeks bulging like two buns. The Shens' gate still lay in Ahe's family's plot.

Xiaoman's mother crouched and picked up the pieces of the bowl one by one. His father stood by rubbing his hands. "Wife… a broken bowl, we can buy another…" His mother said, "With what?"

His father said, "…With… with my knee?" His mother said, "What's your knee worth?" His father gave it serious thought. "On cloudy days it's pretty accurate. Could be a weather forecast."

His mother didn't laugh. She just crouched there with a piece of the bowl in her hand, and for a long while didn't move. His father stopped talking too, slowly crouched beside her, and picked up the pieces with her. The two of them picked them up one by one, very, very slowly, as if, picked up any faster, the bowl would really be gone.

Those seven or eight pieces his mother wrapped in an old cloth, tied the four corners, did not throw away, and put in the wooden chest at the head of the kang. What a broken bowl was good for, nobody asked that day.

That night Xiaoman said to the hole in the roof, very, very quietly: "One day I'll make it so my mother never has to crouch on the floor picking things up again." The roof, naturally, didn't answer; only a drop of rain leaked through and fell into the seventeenth basin in the corner — *ding*.

Through the cloth curtain his parents were talking low.

His father said, "…When's the Start of Winter?" His mother said, "The day after the day after tomorrow." A pause. "Three days left." His father said, "The front hills are empty. There's only Black Pine Ridge." It was quiet behind the curtain a good while; then his mother said, "Your father — Black Pine Ridge is where he was lost." His father said, "I know."

His mother said no more. After a while she cried a little, and then stopped.

Xiaoman lay on the kang and went over the account, item by item — his mother had taught him that: when something happens, first work out the sums.

Ma Xiaobao was a head taller and twice his weight — in a fight, he'd lose. Even if he won, Ma San stood in the doorway — in a fight, his father would be the one beaten. Even if he beat Ma San as well… Xiaoman pictured it: twelve-year-old Shen Xiaoman knocking a door flat with one punch.

He felt this "even if" was a little far off. So today he hadn't hit back — only talked back once. Talking back isn't hitting back; that was a rule he'd made for himself.

He lay with his eyes open in the dark and set it all down, item by item: the shove Ma Xiaobao gave him, the way Ma San looked at the bow, the bowl that went flying, and his mother's hand stopped in mid-air. Ma San, Ma Xiaobao, Master Ma, and Master Ma's distant nephew the clerk — in his head he cursed them all once more, one by one: **Your grandpa's.**

That done, he said four words to himself: **Can't beat them now.** Then he said the last word over again on its own: **Now.**

In the middle of the night there was a rustling behind the curtain; his father went out in the dark, and came back with something heavy, which he set on the threshold — *thunk*. Then came *shh, shh, shh*, one stroke after another, slow and even: iron on stone.

The Shens' whetstone had split in two the year before last; this one must have been borrowed from somebody. Xiaoman counted the strokes, got past three hundred, lost count, and gave up. He knew what his father was sharpening. The front hills were empty, and a deer had to be got within three days: what his father was sharpening were arrows for the deep mountains.

exits.means: hits back, clenches fists, tries to fight Ma Xiaobao

what.zh: 要拿走爷爷的弓；那一棍落在爹肩上。
what.en: Means to take grandfather's bow; his club came down on your father's shoulder.

马三一挥手，带着马小宝走了。临出门时，马小宝回过头来，冲小满挤了挤眼睛，当着他的面，把那块桂花糕一口塞进嘴里，腮帮子鼓得像两个包子。沈家的门，还躺在阿禾家的菜地里。

他娘没有笑。她就那么蹲着，手里捏着一片碗，许久没有动。他爹也不说话了，慢慢地蹲下去，挨着她，和她一起捡。两个人一片一片，捡得极慢极慢，倒像是捡得快了，那只碗便当真没了。

那只碗的七八片，他娘拿一块旧布包了，四个角系好，没有扔，收进了炕头的木箱里。一只碎了的碗，留着能做什么，那天谁也没有问，她自己大约也说不上来。

隔着一道布帘，爹娘在低声说话。

他爹道：「……立冬是哪天？」他娘道：「大后天。」停了一停，又道：「还剩三天。」他爹道：「前山空了。只剩黑松岭。」布帘那边静了好一会儿，他娘道：「你爹，就是在黑松岭没的。」他爹道：「我知道。」他娘便不说了。

过了一会儿，她哭了一小会儿，又不哭了。

那一夜他没怎么睡。他在心里把账算了一遍：马小宝比他高一个头，重他一倍；门口站着马三，马三手里有棍子。他松开了拳头，是对的——他爹肩膀上那一棍，比他那一拳贵。

他在黑暗里睁着眼睛，把马小宝推他那一下，马三瞧那张弓的眼神，那只飞出去的碗，还有他娘停在半空的手，一样一样都记了下来。马三，马小宝，马家老爷，还有马家老爷那个做书吏的远房表侄，他在心里又挨个儿骂了一遍：**你爷爷的。**

骂完了，又对自己说了五个字：**现在打不过。**说完一遍，又单把末了两个字念了一遍：**现在。**

到了半夜，布帘那边窸窸窣窣一阵响，他爹摸黑出去了，回来时手里多了一样沉甸甸的东西，搁在门槛上，「咚」的一声。跟着便是「嚓、嚓、嚓」，一声一声，又慢又匀，是铁在石头上磨。

沈家的磨刀石前年便裂成了两半，这一块，不知是打哪家借来的。小满数着那「嚓嚓」声，数到三百多下，数乱了，便不数了。他知道他爹在磨什么。前山已经空了，三天里要打着一头鹿，他爹磨的，是进深山的箭。
story.en:
Xiaoman clenched his fists.

His father was quicker. Still on his knees he shuffled forward, right in front of his son, blocking him off completely. "Third Master, the boy's young. He doesn't know better."

Ma San's club came down on his father's shoulder with a dull thud. His father swayed, made no sound, and kept the smile on his face — a smile uglier than crying. "Third Master has a fine strong arm."

Xiaoman's fists loosened, bit by bit. But Ma Xiaobao hadn't had his fill; he lunged and shoved him hard.

Xiaoman fell backwards. In the instant of falling a great many things flashed through his head: the short, poor twelve years of his life, his father's knee, his mother's hands, the old locust tree at the village gate he'd climbed a hundred times, and the four bowls on the stove.

A thousand threads, and by the time they reached his lips only one was left; he didn't dare say it aloud, but in his head he cursed it at the top of his voice: **Your grandpa's.**

Pain in his back — he'd struck the stove, and with a *crack* the bowl on its edge was jolted off and went tumbling head over heels through the air. The setting sun slanted in through the doorway just then; a flash of white ran round the bowl's rim, as though it were saying goodbye.

Xiaoman grabbed for it, quick as you like, and his fingertips just reached the bottom of it — and fell short by an inch.

*Crash* — the bowl broke into seven or eight pieces on the floor.

Xiaoman lay flat on his back, staring up at the hole in the roof, and for a moment forgot to get up. Just then a drop of rain leaked through the hole and landed squarely between his eyebrows, cold. He sighed at the roof and said, "That was the only one of our four bowls without a chip."

Ma San waved a hand and went, taking Ma Xiaobao with him. At the door Ma Xiaobao turned, winked at Xiaoman, and right in front of him stuffed the whole osmanthus cake into his mouth, cheeks bulging like two buns. The Shens' gate still lay in Ahe's family's plot.

His mother didn't laugh. She just crouched there with a piece of the bowl in her hand, and for a long, long while didn't move. His father stopped talking too, slowly crouched beside her — rubbing the shoulder the club had found — and picked up the pieces with her. The two of them picked them up one by one, very, very slowly, as if, picked up any faster, the bowl would really be gone.

The seven or eight pieces of that bowl his mother wrapped in an old cloth, tied the four corners, did not throw away, and put in the wooden chest at the head of the kang. What a broken bowl was good for, nobody asked that day; she probably couldn't have said herself.

Through the cloth curtain his parents were talking low.

His father said, "…When's the Start of Winter?" His mother said, "The day after the day after tomorrow." A pause. "Three days left." His father said, "The front hills are empty. There's only Black Pine Ridge." It was quiet behind the curtain a good while; then his mother said, "Your father — Black Pine Ridge is where he was lost." His father said, "I know."

His mother said no more. After a while she cried a little, and then stopped.

He barely slept that night. He went over the account in his head: Ma Xiaobao a head taller and twice his weight; Ma San in the doorway with his club. Loosening his fists had been right — the blow on his father's shoulder cost more than his punch was worth.

He lay with his eyes open in the dark and set it all down, item by item: the shove Ma Xiaobao gave him, the way Ma San looked at the bow, the bowl that went flying, and his mother's hand stopped in mid-air. Ma San, Ma Xiaobao, Master Ma, and Master Ma's distant nephew the clerk — in his head he cursed them all once more, one by one: **Your grandpa's.**

That done, he said four words to himself: **Can't beat them now.** Then he said the last word over again on its own: **Now.**

In the middle of the night there was a rustling behind the curtain; his father went out in the dark, and came back with something heavy, which he set on the threshold — *thunk*. Then came *shh, shh, shh*, one stroke after another, slow and even: iron on stone.

The Shens' whetstone had split in two the year before last; this one must have been borrowed from somebody. Xiaoman counted the strokes, got past three hundred, lost count, and gave up. He knew what his father was sharpening. The front hills were empty, and a deer had to be got within three days: what his father was sharpening were arrows for the deep mountains.
